strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and practically motivated inverse problem in which the forward operator is discrete and non-differentiable, making conventional diffusion posterior guidance difficult.

The cross-modal contrastive guidance idea is intuitive and potentially useful beyond floorplan reconstruction. Replacing explicit path-planner differentiation with a learned compatibility energy is a sensible design direction.

The experiments compare against several planner-based DPS variants, generic diffusion inverse solvers, and a conditional diffusion baseline. The reported synthetic-data improvements over the inverse-solver baselines are substantial.

The paper includes useful qualitative results, trajectory-density experiments, a noise stress test, and ablations of the intersection weight and optimizer. The architecture and training appendix provides some implementation information.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is overstated. The likelihood-ratio interpretation of InfoNCE holds under an idealized optimum and sampling assumptions; finite-capacity unit-normalized encoders with bounded cosine similarity need not represent the true log-density ratio. Moreover, the actual objective adds multi-positive, alignment, and directional terms, so its optimum is not the stated InfoNCE optimum. The assertion that multi-positive training becomes single-positive merely because inference supplies one observation is not a valid justification.

Smoothness and stability are asserted rather than established. Neural encoders are not automatically Lipschitz or guaranteed to yield well-behaved gradients, and the floorplan encoder is trained on clean binary layouts but differentiated on continuous, partially denoised estimates during sampling. There is no gradient-norm, landscape, or robustness analysis demonstrating that this surrogate is smoother than the planner objectives.

The evaluation is entirely synthetic: both training and testing use A*-generated trajectories on low-resolution, furniture-free HouseExpo layouts. No human trajectories, real localization measurements, alternative navigation policies, cross-dataset tests, or simulator-mismatch experiments are included. Consequently, the practical claims about reconstructing homes from user movement are not supported.

Important evaluation information is missing or inconsistent. The paper does not report the number of evaluated test cases or statistical significance, and the density description calls approximately 40%, 25%, and 10% coverage sparse, moderate, and dense, respectively, apparently reversing the labels. F1 and IoU are nearly redundant, while direct trajectory consistency, wall-intersection rate, connectivity, structural validity, and perceptual plausibility are not quantitatively evaluated despite being central to the motivation.

The ablations do not isolate the main methodological choices: symmetric versus one-way contrastive training, alignment loss, multi-positive training, temperature, guidance schedule, clean-versus-noisy encoder inputs, and contrastive guidance versus the hand-designed intersection penalty. The only strong end-to-end conditional baseline, CFG, outperforms CoGuide in the dense regime, and comparison with prior embedding- or classifier-energy-guided diffusion methods is missing.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The repository field is blank; several settings are given as ranges or optional choices rather than the exact configuration used. Critical inference parameters such as Adam learning rate and gating thresholds are not specified. Algorithm 1 also omits a gradient on the intersection term and leaves its optimization sign ambiguous, while the appendix contrastive equations contain inconsistent encoder arguments and indexing.

The uncertainty study uses only five samples and provides no calibration or coverage evaluation. The retrieval visualization includes the ground-truth floorplan itself as the top result, making that result largely tautological.

The claim that trajectories are privacy-preserving is unsubstantiated and questionable, since movement traces can expose spatial layout and occupant behavior. Privacy and misuse implications are not discussed. Overall, the promising idea is not supported by sufficiently sound theory, realistic validation, or reproducible experimentation for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting inverse problem in which the forward operator is discrete and non-differentiable, and proposes an intuitive cross-modal contrastive guidance mechanism.
The manuscript is generally well organized and includes comparisons with six baselines, qualitative examples, measurement-noise experiments, and ablations of the intersection penalty and optimizer.
On the synthetic HouseExpo benchmark, CoGuide substantially outperforms planner-based DPS variants and generic inverse solvers, with its largest advantage over CFG in the sparse-trajectory regime.

The use of a generative prior is appropriate for the inherently ambiguous mapping from trajectories to layouts. weaknesses: The central practical claim is supported only by synthetic A*-generated trajectories on low-resolution, furniture-free HouseExpo layouts. There are no human trajectories, realistic IMU localization errors, alternative navigation policies, or cross-dataset tests. Training and evaluation therefore share essentially the same synthetic measurement process, leaving real-world validity unestablished.

The theoretical justification is overstated. The InfoNCE density-ratio result holds at an ideal optimum with sufficiently expressive scoring and the specified negative distribution; it does not establish that the learned, bounded dot-product score is the true likelihood. The added multi-positive, alignment, and directional objectives further change that result. The assertion that the training objective becomes single-positive merely because inference supplies one measurement is not valid.

Smoothness is asserted rather than demonstrated. Ordinary neural encoders are not automatically usefully Lipschitz, no Lipschitz constraint or Jacobian bound is imposed, and there is no empirical comparison of guidance-gradient norms or stability. Moreover, the floorplan encoder is trained on clean binary images but applied during sampling to noisy, continuous Tweedie estimates; the appendix says diffusion-style corruption was disabled, creating a consequential distribution shift.

The evaluation metrics are inadequate for floorplan reconstruction. Free-space IoU and F1 are dominated by large interior regions and do not measure wall-boundary accuracy, connectivity, room topology, path feasibility, or trajectory collisions. The qualitative results show substantial structural mismatches despite high scores, illustrating this metric weakness.

The strongest baseline, CFG, already matches or exceeds CoGuide: it is better in the dense regime and trails by only 0.01 F1 in the moderate regime. There is no statistical significance analysis, sample count, direct supervised predictor, retrieval baseline, conditional diffusion baseline beyond CFG, or comparison to the most relevant floorplan-from-trajectory method. Baseline training budgets, capacity, tuning effort, and use of the intersection constraint are also insufficiently controlled.

Several methodological details are questionable or ambiguous. Algorithm 1 appears to add the intersection cost with a positive sign despite describing it as a penalty to minimize; the exact update convention is unclear. Adam is incorrectly characterized as supplying higher-order information. The stated mapping of sparse, moderate, and dense trajectories to 40%, 25%, and 10% coverage appears reversed.

The uncertainty experiment uses only five samples and reports an uncalibrated variance visualization. It does not test coverage, calibration, posterior correctness, or whether multiple plausible layouts are represented, so it cannot substantiate uncertainty-quantification claims.

Reproducibility is below the expected standard: the repository link is absent, and the appendix gives ranges or optional choices rather than the exact configuration used. Important guidance weights, annealing and stopping settings, temperatures, batch/evaluation sizes, checkpoint selection, EMA choice, and baseline configurations are missing or ambiguous.

The broader novelty is only moderate: the method resembles learned energy/contrastive or CLIP-style guidance for diffusion, but that literature is not adequately compared or positioned. Evidence is confined to one operator and dataset, so claims about a broader family of spatial, blind, molecular, or network inverse problems are speculative.

The claim that motion trajectories are privacy-preserving is unsupported and potentially misleading: indoor trajectories and inferred floorplans are themselves sensitive data with surveillance and security implications, yet the paper provides no meaningful privacy, misuse, or ethical analysis.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and practically motivated idea: replacing gradients through a discontinuous path planner with guidance from a jointly learned floorplan–trajectory embedding. This is an intuitive and potentially reusable approach for inverse problems with non-differentiable forward operators.

The method is technically coherent and integrates contrastive learning with diffusion posterior sampling in a straightforward way. The paper also explains the instability of planner-based guidance well and provides useful visual evidence of it.

The main experiment is reasonably broad, covering six baselines, three trajectory-density regimes, measurement noise, qualitative examples, and ablations of the intersection penalty and optimizer. CoGuide substantially outperforms the planner-based inverse solvers and is competitive with or better than CFG in sparse and moderate regimes.

The appendix provides architectural details, additional qualitative results, planner descriptions, and an initial uncertainty analysis. The presentation is generally clear and the application is interesting.
weaknesses: All evidence is based on synthetic A*-generated trajectories over low-resolution, furniture-free HouseExpo layouts. There are no human trajectories, reconstructed IMU trajectories, realistic localization errors, or cross-dataset tests. Consequently, the claimed practical relevance to recovering real homes from user movement is not convincingly established.

The theoretical justification is overstated. InfoNCE recovers a density ratio only at the population optimum under assumptions about positive and negative sampling; this does not establish that the learned finite-capacity encoders provide an accurate likelihood score. Moreover, the floorplan encoder is trained on clean binary layouts but is differentiated on intermediate Tweedie estimates during sampling, and this distribution shift is neither analyzed nor controlled—the optional diffusion corruption is explicitly disabled.

Evaluation with free-space IoU and F1 against a single ground-truth floorplan is inadequate for an explicitly ill-posed, multimodal problem and can be dominated by large open regions. The paper lacks wall-focused metrics, path feasibility or forward-consistency measurements, posterior coverage/calibration, and evaluation of whether alternative valid layouts are generated.

The comparison does not fully isolate the contribution. CFG is the most relevant learned conditional baseline and decisively wins in the dense regime, while CoGuide also requires paired floorplan–trajectory data. Data-efficiency, out-of-distribution generalization, and robustness to changes in the trajectory-generating policy are not tested, so the practical advantage over ordinary conditional generation remains unclear.

Several crucial ablations are missing, including contrastive guidance versus direct compatibility regression, alignment loss, symmetric versus one-directional objectives, clean versus noise-augmented encoder training, annealing and hard gating, temperature, and guidance strength. The provided ablations cover only two auxiliary implementation choices.

Baseline adaptation and statistical reporting need more detail. It is unclear how DiffPIR and DMPlug are given a suitable measurement objective, planner baselines optimize different proxy outputs, the number of evaluated examples and random seeds is not reported, and no significance analysis is provided.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed: the appendix frequently gives ranges or optional settings rather than the exact configuration used, and important inference and data-generation hyperparameters are missing. There are also notation swaps in the appendix's encoder/loss descriptions and no usable anonymous repository link in the submitted manuscript.

The statement that trajectories are privacy-preserving is questionable, since movement traces can reveal both spatial layout and sensitive behavioral information. The paper would benefit from an explicit privacy and misuse discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and practically motivated inverse problem involving a partially known, non-differentiable path-planning operator.

Using a jointly learned contrastive embedding to guide an unconditional diffusion prior is intuitive, potentially reusable, and meaningfully different from directly differentiating through a path planner.

The synthetic floorplan experiments compare against several relevant diffusion and path-planning baselines and report substantial improvements, especially for CoGuide combined with classifier-free guidance.
The paper includes useful robustness and optimization studies covering trajectory density, measurement noise, the intersection penalty, and Adam versus gradient descent.
The qualitative real-sensor experiment and audio-restoration extension are valuable attempts to test applicability beyond the primary synthetic setting.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is overstated. The InfoNCE density-ratio identity holds only under idealized assumptions about the negative distribution, scoring-function capacity, and attainment of the population optimum. Here the score is a bounded normalized inner product and training additionally uses multi-positive supervision, alignment, and directional losses. These changes generally do not preserve the asserted equality to the likelihood score; observing one measurement at inference does not make the training objective revert to single-positive InfoNCE.

The assertion that the learned guidance is smooth and stable is not established. Neural encoders are not automatically suitably Lipschitz, and the floorplan encoder is trained on clean binary images but differentiated on noisy, continuous Tweedie estimates during sampling; the stated diffusion-style corruption is disabled in the main training. No gradient-norm, smoothness, or off-manifold analysis addresses this mismatch.

Most evidence uses A*-generated trajectories for both learning and evaluation, so strong results may reflect learning the same synthetic generator rather than handling unknown human navigation. The real-world study contains only two apartments, is qualitative, and lacks comparisons with specialized trajectory-to-floorplan approaches such as Walk2Map.

Evaluation relies on free-space pixel F1 and IoU, which can be dominated by large open regions and do not adequately measure wall topology, room connectivity, trajectory consistency, or posterior quality. Test-set sample counts and statistical testing are absent, and scoring an intrinsically ambiguous posterior against one ground-truth layout is insufficiently discussed.

The ablations do not isolate several essential design choices: contrastive guidance versus a directly learned compatibility/regression loss, symmetric versus one-directional training, multi-positive training, the alignment term, clean versus diffusion-corrupted encoder inputs, or guidance hyperparameters. Consequently, it is unclear which claimed methodological components cause the gains.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistencies and underspecification. The text associates sparse, moderate, and dense trajectories with 40%, 25%, and 10% coverage in that order, apparently reversing the labels. Appendix loss equations mix up the floorplan and trajectory encoders and appear to use incorrect denominator indices. Several training details are given as ranges or optional settings rather than the exact configuration used for reported results.

The audio experiment does not convincingly support the broad blind-inverse-problem claim: it compares only with a weak spectral equalization baseline, omits stronger restoration methods and detailed test-set statistics, and uses FAD rather than paired reconstruction/fidelity measures. Training on a predefined synthetic degradation family also limits the claim of handling fully unknown operators.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and difficult inverse problem in which the forward process is discrete, partially known, and unsuitable for ordinary gradient-based diffusion guidance.
Using a contrastively learned cross-modal compatibility function as diffusion guidance is intuitive and potentially useful beyond floorplan reconstruction.

The synthetic floorplan experiments cover several trajectory densities, multiple diffusion/path-planning baselines, measurement noise, and some useful ablations. CoGuide substantially outperforms the operator-based DPS variants and improves over CFG in the sparse regime.
The paper includes a small real-world demonstration and an exploratory audio application, which help illustrate the intended broader scope.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is overstated. The InfoNCE density-ratio identity holds for the population optimum under a particular negative-sampling distribution and sufficiently expressive scoring function; it does not establish that the trained finite-capacity encoders recover the likelihood score, especially for off-manifold intermediate diffusion estimates.

The extension to supervised multi-positive contrastive learning is not justified. The claim that it becomes ordinary single-positive InfoNCE because only one measurement is supplied at inference confuses the inference input with the training objective; the learned score is determined by the multi-positive training distribution.

Smooth neural encoders do not by themselves guarantee Lipschitz, stable, or likelihood-faithful gradients. No empirical analysis directly measures gradient smoothness, calibration against a known likelihood, or robustness to off-manifold denoising states, despite these being central motivations.

The evaluation is dominated by trajectories synthetically generated with A* from the same dataset used to train the compatibility model. This tests interpolation under a chosen simulator more than recovery under an unknown human path-generation process.

Real-world evidence is only qualitative and covers two apartments. There are no quantitative reconstruction metrics, comparisons with established trajectory-based mapping methods such as Walk2Map, repeated users, diverse buildings, or meaningful robustness analysis for human behavior and sensor/domain shift.

The strongest reported result comes from CFG+CoGuide, which combines two separately trained conditioning mechanisms and additional computation. Its improvement over CFG does not isolate the contribution of the proposed surrogate, while CoGuide alone is worse than CFG in the dense regime.

Several baselines are weakly or unusually adapted: generic restoration solvers lack their standard measurement proximal, DiPPeR is reimplemented without official code, and the paper does not establish equal tuning or compute budgets. This makes the large baseline gaps difficult to interpret.

Important ablations are missing, including contrastive loss versus the alignment term, symmetric versus one-way training, embedding dimension and temperature, negative construction, trajectory augmentations, guidance schedule, and a simple direct conditional/retrieval-based predictor.

The audio extension is preliminary and does not support the broad blind-inverse-problem claim. It trains on a known synthetic degradation family, compares against only one restoration baseline, reports no sample count or reconstruction-fidelity metric, and does not clearly demonstrate generalization to genuinely unknown degradations.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the stated commitment: the repository link is blank, many settings are presented as ranges or optional choices rather than the exact configuration used, and crucial inference hyperparameters are not fully specified. There are also internal inconsistencies, such as sparse/moderate/dense coverage being listed as 40%/25%/10%, apparent encoder-variable swaps in the appendix equations, and ambiguous guidance-gating descriptions.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful and challenging inverse-problem regime: partially specified, non-differentiable forward operators. Replacing direct operator gradients with contrastive embedding-space guidance is intuitive, useful, and sufficiently distinct from standard diffusion posterior sampling.
The floorplan application is well motivated, and the method combines a learned diffusion prior with measurement compatibility without requiring a differentiable path planner at inference time.

The main synthetic evaluation is broad: CoGuide is compared with three planner-based DPS variants, two established inverse solvers, and classifier-free guidance across three trajectory-density regimes. CoGuide is particularly effective for sparse trajectories, while CFG+CoGuide achieves the strongest reported results throughout.

The paper includes useful qualitative comparisons, robustness experiments under measurement noise, an optimizer ablation, an intersection-penalty sweep, uncertainty visualizations, and a small real-world UWB demonstration.
The blind-audio experiment provides encouraging evidence that the core idea may transfer beyond floorplans, although this evidence remains preliminary.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and supported by extensive architectural and training information in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is overstated. The InfoNCE density-ratio result holds at an ideal population optimum with sufficient function capacity and a specific negative-sampling distribution. Unit-normalized finite-dimensional embeddings constrain the representable ratio, and the added alignment and supervised multi-positive losses change the optimum. The claim that multi-positive training simply reduces to single-positive InfoNCE because only one measurement is supplied at inference is not valid. Thus, the method is a plausible learned surrogate, but it is not shown to recover the true likelihood score as claimed.

The paper motivates the method through smoother and more stable gradients, yet does not directly measure gradient norms, Lipschitz behavior, score approximation error, convergence stability, or sensitivity relative to planner-based guidance. Such evidence would substantially strengthen the central mechanism claim.

The evaluation metrics operate on free-space pixels and can be dominated by large open regions, while thin walls, connectivity, room topology, and trajectory-wall consistency are central to the application. Boundary-aware, structural, connectivity, and path-validity metrics are needed. Test-set sample counts, confidence intervals or significance tests are also absent.

The real-world evidence consists of only two apartments and is purely qualitative. It is therefore too limited to support strong claims of real-world generalization, especially under changes in building style, localization noise, furniture, and human behavior.

Several important component ablations are missing, including contrastive losses versus alignment, annealing and hard gating, learned temperature, encoder design, and CoGuide without Adam-related modifications. Runtime and memory comparisons are also absent, despite backpropagation through the denoiser and encoder during sampling.

The trajectory-density description appears inconsistent: sparse, moderate, and dense are associated with 40%, 25%, and 10% of open space, respectively. The construction of trajectories and exact evaluation protocol need clarification to rule out labeling or reporting errors.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The anonymous repository link is blank, and several decisive inference parameters are given as ranges or options rather than exact values, including guidance learning rates, annealing boundaries, stopping time, loss weights, and evaluation sampling settings. There are also notation inconsistencies in the appendix where the floorplan and trajectory encoders are swapped.

The audio extension is under-evaluated: it uses only one substantive baseline, omits test-set size and uncertainty, and trains on a specified family of synthetic degradations. This does not yet establish performance on genuinely unknown or out-of-distribution degradation operators, so the broad blind-inverse-problem claim should be presented as preliminary.
